item.description: Minority and underserved youth are less likely to undergo diabetic retinopathy screening, yet more likely to have diabetic retinopathy. We hypothesize that autonomous artificial intelligence-based diabetic eye exams could mitigate screening disparities in minority youth. This prospective study enrolled 397 White and non-White youth with type 1 (72%) and type 2 (28%) diabetes at diabetes care visits. Participants underwent autonomous artificial-intelligence diabetic eye exams and optical coherence tomography imaging. The primary outcome is equivalence in screening completion between White and non-White youth. The secondary outcome is diagnostic accuracy of AI against prognostic standard. At baseline, participants in the White cohort were more likely to have completed a prior diabetic eye exam (79.8% v 61.8%, p < 0.0001). Following the artificial-intelligence intervention, 99.5% in the White cohort and 98% in the non-White cohort completed the autonomous artificial-intelligence diabetic eye exam, demonstrating equivalent screening completion after implementation. item.description: While clinical guidelines remain essential for standardizing medical care, their utility decays as manual updating fails to keep pace with the exponential growth in medical evidence. To address this challenge, we developed a Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MARG) system dedicated to clinical guideline development and maintenance. We employed a multi-phase evaluation framework to assess MARG’s performance across agent-agent interaction and human-AI collaboration tasks. The system was evaluated against seven 2025 liver disease guidelines, encompassing 137 clinical scenarios. Here we show MARG achieve 77.4% overall concordance with the guidelines, with consistency rates rising from 45.8% under weak consensus to 87.8% at full consensus. Domain-specific performance is 65.5% for diagnosis, 75.0% for prevention, and 81.0% for treatment. MARG also assists in evidence integration, outperforming manual review in recency (6.3% vs. 0.9%), reproducibility (25.5% vs. 7.5%), and quality (24.2% vs. 8.0% Level I evidence).
